https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw98.text: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, Tukaram Mundhe has led a series of enforcement drives since taking charge in May By Nikita Yadav BBC News, Delhi Published 3 hours ago Among the thousands of civil servants who keep India's vast government machinery running, a small number become unlikely public figures every few years. Tukaram Mundhe, 51, is one of them. The commissioner of Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration, he has led a series of enforcement drives since taking charge in May. His teams have inspected restaurants and other food businesses, uncovering pest infestations, poor hygiene and expired food. He has also highlighted large gaps between what hospitals pay for common medical supplies and what patients are charged. These actions have made Mundhe a social-media celebrity, with videos and images from inspections widely shared online. Hundreds of people have commented that they wished officers like him could be sent to fix food safety concerns in their state. Mundhe is not alone. In Gurugram, a suburb of Delhi, district town planner RS Batth has won praise for acting against illegal construction and encroachments. But why are these officials treated like heroes for doing their jobs? In India, civil servants are responsible for many services people rely on every day, from issuing documents to policing, food safety and healthcare. But many are also accused of delays, bribes and making people run from pillar to post. So when an official appears to cut through the red tape, the response can be surprisingly enthusiastic. "What should have been normal has become exceptional," says retired civil servant Kamal Kant Jaswal. For many citizens, delays, bureaucratic hurdles and indifferent treatment have become so familiar that efficient governance now stands out as an exception, he adds. Image source, The Washington Post via Getty Images Image caption, Many Indians associate government offices with lengthy procedures, repeated visits and an often-unresponsive bureaucracy Mundhe is not the first official to gain recognition for doing exactly that. One of the most prominent examples is TN Seshan, who became a household name as India's chief election commissioner in the 1990s for fearlessly enforcing rules. Kiran Bedi , the first woman to join the officer ranks of the Indian Police Service, was nicknamed "Crane Bedi" in the early 1980s after it was widely reported that she got an illegally parked car belonging to then prime minister Indira Gandhi towed away (it was removed by a sub-inspector who reported to her, who said years later that she supported , external his decision). Ashok Khemka became nationally known after intervening in a controversial land transaction in 2012, while police officer Neeraj Jadaun was praised for confronting a mob during deadly religious violence in Delhi in 2020. These stories have made the idea of the "honest" or "no-nonsense" bureaucrat both familiar and rare. Jaswal, however, points out that thousands of officials in India do their jobs without attracting public attention. "Their work may not involve much direct contact with citizens, or may simply be less visible." For ordinary people, however, a visit to a government office is often seen as an exhausting process. Rajesh Singh, 43, who works at a finance company in Delhi, says he has experienced long waits to get his work done and even longer processes to solve complaints. "What is supposed to take 24 hours, I have personally experienced being stretched to six months with no guarantee of a positive outcome even then," he says. But an officer praised for enforcing rules can also face criticism for applying them too rigidly without taking into account ground realities. Image source, The India Today Group via Getty Images Image caption, Kiran Bedi, India's first woman IPS officer, became known for her strict approach to law enforcement Mundhe has been criticised by sections of the food and hospitality industry over his enforcement drives. He has rejected allegations of selective or unlawful action, saying inspections are evidence-driven and licences are suspended only in serious cases. Batth, too, has faced flak for acting against illegal encroachments, with critics alleging his enforcement is selective and disproportionately affects vulnerable people. In several viral videos, he has said his actions are carried out strictly under town-planning rules. Jaswal explains a street vendor's stall may be an unauthorised structure in the eyes of the law, but could be a family's only source of income. And in a country where millions migrate to cities in search of work, unsanctioned living spaces could be the only way to find a place to stay. This tension between the law and economics helps explain why the same enforcement action can be viewed as both lawful and harsh. Bureaucrats also face challenges of their own while carrying out their duties. Pushpa Sundar, who briefly served as a civil servant and has written extensively on development issues, says officers can face political pressure and transfers when they refuse to comply with demands. "They too have families, careers and financial responsibilities and it needs extraordinary courage to risk those things in order to act independently," she says. She argues that officers need stronger institutional support when they refuse to do something illegal or improper. Jaswal remembers facing such pressure himself. In 1974, when he was district magistrate of Uttarkashi in what was then undivided Uttar Pradesh, a senior minister was contesting the state legislature election. He says he had to turn down a number of demands from the minister as they were against the rules. The minister won the election and Jaswal says he got his "marching orders soon after". But when he left for his next assignment, people stood in the summer heat for several kilometres on his way to say goodbye. The relationship between politicians and civil servants, he says, is rarely straightforward. Many civil servants who seek desirable postings or rely on political support choose the path of least resistance, while standing up to political pressure entails certain costs, he says. Image source, Kamal Kant Jaswal Image caption, Kamal Kant Jaswal (right) with former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi during his tenure as Uttar Pradesh's secretary for rural development. Social media has also changed how quickly an officer can become a public sensation. An action once limited to a district can now be filmed, shared and viewed by millions within hours. "Social media can turn an official into a national talking point almost overnight," Sundar says. That is partly what happened with Mundhe, whose inspection videos have turned routine enforcement into a widely watched spectacle. Mundhe, however, sees it differently. Speaking to the BBC last month, he said his actions were driven by public-health concerns and that businesses complying with rules had nothing to fear. For Mundhe, the attention is beside the point. The rules already exist and his job is simply to enforce them. But the public fascination is about more than just one officer. When basic government functions are carried out visibly and consistently, they can seem extraordinary - particularly because so many people have come to expect otherwise. https://www.naturalnews.com/2026-09-24-p.text: Poland's Border Guard identified 8,300 illegal foreign residents from January through August 2026, a 40% jump over the same period last year. Ukrainians and Colombians make up the largest shares of those detained, followed by Georgians, Belarusians and Moldovans. Experts warn Poland is entering a full-scale crisis as forged documents, informal rentals and shell companies let migrants operate outside the law. Unregistered foreigners pose added security risks, officials say, since they are harder to track and could be exploited for sabotage or other hostile activity. The overstay surge stands in sharp contrast to Poland's success sealing new Belarus border crossings, which collapsed from 15,500 to just 235 this year. Poland's Border Guard has identified approximately 8,300 foreigners living illegally in the country between January and the end of August 2026, marking a roughly 40% increase from the approximately 6,000 detected during the same period last year. The sharp rise has prompted security experts to warn that Warsaw is entering what one professor called a "full-scale crisis" in managing foreign populations already inside its territory. Ukrainians account for 2,200 of those detained, while Colombians represent 1,400, followed by Georgians at 748, Belarusians at 400, and Moldovans at 354, according to Major Anna Sobieska-Tekie?, spokesperson for Border Guard Headquarters. Many of these individuals lack documents permitting them to stay in Poland or have overstayed their legal residence periods. Extensive shadow networks enable illegal work and housing A sophisticated support infrastructure allows foreigners to operate outside Poland's legal framework, including forged visas and work permits, informal apartment rentals, and fictitious companies created specifically to obtain work visas for migrants, according to Polish news outlet Rzeczpospolita. Tomasz Safja?ski, a professor at WSB University in D?browa GÃ³rnicza and deputy director of the Center for Research on Cross-Border Security, warned that when a state controls its border but loses the ability to determine who remains after residence rights expire, a "security gap" emerges. Experts point to a growing shadow economy where illegal employment allows employers to avoid taxes and social-security contributions, while raising the risk of organized crime including human trafficking and document forgery. Intelligence concerns grow over unmonitored foreign populations People who remain outside Poland's official registration system pose particular security risks. Officials interviewed by Rzeczpospolita said such individuals are harder to track and could be exploited by foreign intelligence services to carry out sabotage or other hostile operations. The Polish Border Guard runs ongoing enforcement sweeps targeting people who have exceeded their permitted residence period, are working without the required permit, are using invalid documents, or were previously barred from Poland or other Schengen countries; officers also detain people who had earlier been ordered to leave the European Union. Crackdown operations expand nationwide In an earlier nationwide operation conducted March 2â3, Polish police and Border Guard deployed more than 26,000 officers in a two-day sweep targeting wanted foreign nationals. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski reported that 147 foreigners wanted by Polish law enforcement were detained, with 140 identified as staying illegally. Return proceedings were initiated against over 130 of those detained, with illegal stay cited as the reason in nearly 110 cases and national security threats cited in over 20 cases. The largest groups checked were from Ukraine, Colombia, and Nepal. This marked the fourth such operation, following 2025 raids that detained 4,766 people including 515 foreigners. Between January 1 and March 1, Poland also transferred 33 foreigners back to Lithuania and 13 to Germany under readmission procedures. The accelerating crisis underscores what security analysts describe as Poland's deteriorating ability to track and manage foreign populations already within its borders â a gap that stands in sharp contrast to Warsaw's success at sealing new entries. Attempted illegal crossings from Belarus collapsed from roughly 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to just 235 in the same period this year, according to Poland's Border Guard, after the country built a 5.5-meter steel fence and deployed thousands of additional troops along the frontier. Without comparable resources devoted to interior enforcement, migrants who arrive through legal channels or slip through gaps in an overwhelmed visa and residency system appear increasingly free to vanish into the shadow economy once they are inside the country. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg.text: Image source, Ksenia Arkhipova Image caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year By Jaroslav Lukiv Â and Â Bernd Debusmann Jr ,Â White House reporter Published 23 October 2026, 15:13 BST Updated 1 hour ago US First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said. It said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" without medicine, food and clean water would begin on 29 October. Ukraine and Russia confirmed the deal was agreed to evacuate residents and deliver aid. They both said their forces would stop firing at 02:00 GMT on 27 October. Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Trapped between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east, residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive. Figure caption, Trump: First lady's 'initiative' led to truce for Ukraine city The White House statement said Melania Trump and one of her representatives had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire". "Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying. "Residents who wish to evacuate will receive co-ordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine." Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible". The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for. Davyd Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads President Volodymyr Zelensky's party in parliament, later said "an operation to unblock the settlement of Oleshky and its surroundings will begin in the near future". "To achieve this goal, a ceasefire will be achieved in the near future, as announced by the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump," he said. In Russia, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman confirmed that, "those who wish to do so will be able to leave this settlement". Image source, Ksenia Arkhipova Image caption, Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutions Last month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water. They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education. Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations. The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months. The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv. Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children. It is also one of a number of settlements where thousands of people lost their homes to a massive flooding caused by the collapse of Nova Khakovka Dam in 2023. Ukraine and its allies accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine. Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, Melania Trump worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to agree the ceasefire, the White House said. While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war. In August 2025, Melania Trump penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide". Although she did not mention Ukraine by name, just days later at the White House Zelensky handed over a letter from his wife Olena, thanking her for her efforts on children. In a rare public appearance in October the same year, the US first lady said that Putin had answered directly in writing and that her representatives were working with the Russian president's team to repatriate Ukrainian children from Russia and vice versa. Some 34 children have reportedly been returned since 2025, including five this July. According to US President Donald Trump, his wife has also privately expressed scepticism about Putin and his desire to achieve peace. "I'd get home, I'd say, 'First lady, I had the most wonderful talk with Vladimir. I think we're finished'," Trump said in July last year. "And then I'll turn on the television, or she'll say to me one time, 'Wow, that's strange because they just bombed a nursing home.'" Photograph: Sam Tabone/WireImage View image in fullscreen Former reality star and wellness influencer Sam Wood had asked the Queensland supreme court to grant him bail as he faces domestic violence charges. Photograph: Sam Tabone/WireImage Queensland Sam Wood to remain in custody after another failed bail bid over domestic violence charges Former Bachelor star and wellness influencer stands accused of choking and assaulting wife at Noosa in Queensland Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Ben Smee Queensland state correspondent Thu 29 Oct 2026 22.47 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 01.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Former Bachelor star Sam Wood will remain in custody while he awaits trial on domestic violence charges , after he was refused bail for a second time. Wood, 46, from Melbourne, has been held in custody since his arrest on 4 October at Noosa. On Friday supreme court justice Patrick McCafferty said Wood posed “an unacceptable risk” of further offending, meaning he will remain in the high-security Wolston correctional centre until his trial, which the court heard might not take place until 2028. Former Bachelor star Sam Wood charged with domestic violence Read more Wood was previously remanded over allegations he choked and assaulted his wife, Snezana Wood, while the family was holidaying on the Sunshine Coast. He is charged with two domestic violence offences: assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation in a domestic setting. His legal team have indicated he will fight the charges and he has not yet entered a plea. During an initial bail hearing, a court heard Snezana was supportive of the charges, that she was allegedly choked and that “there was a cessation of breath”. “She articulates [in a video-recorded statement] the banging of her head on the floor. She couldn’t breathe,” police prosecutor Jeanette Grigoris told the earlier hearing. “She thought she was going to die.” The more serious charge, related to strangulation, placed him in a “show cause” position where there is a presumption against bail unless he can demonstrate he does not pose a risk of re-offending. McCafferty said that Wood had not satisfied him that proposed conditions could ameliorate that risk. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email During Friday’s bail hearing, the Supreme Court heard claims that Wood used drugs and alcohol, engaged in a “party lifestyle” and that he “struggles with anger”. On Friday Wood’s lawyer, Paula Morreau KC, said that there was no suggestion Wood “suffered from addiction” despite crown submissions that he used drugs and alcohol use and engaged in a “party lifestyle”. Morreau said that if granted bail, Wood proposed to reside in Tasmania, where his father lives, and that he would agree to the condition “to not enter Victoria” where Snezana lives. At the earlier application, Wood had sought bail to reside in Melbourne. Sam Wood makes bid for bail to supreme court over domestic violence charges Read more Morreau said Wood had been suffering “significant stressors” and that he “struggles with anger” but that in such situations “he usually leaves and takes time”. “He shows he has the capacity for self-control,” she said. Wood’s legal team proposed he undergo a “men’s behavioural change” course if released on bail. Crown prosecutor Jessica Guy said there were “serious features” to allegations that Wood assaulted and strangled his wife. “[Wood] didn’t desist. [The] violence extended beyond the application of force to her neck, to the banging of her head to the floor of the skirting boards. “[It occurred] in the presence of an adult witness and the close proximity of young children.
